Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The passage over Hawaiʻi is noted.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system exhibited extratropical characteristics despite its tropical origin.
Hazards_Annotation: High winds and heavy rain are typical hazards associated with such systems.

Time_Annotation: July 1971: Hurricane Denise dissipated before reaching Hawaiʻi but brought over an inch of rain and had outer winds affecting the area.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Impacts were noted in Honolulu and nearby agricultural regions in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Denise is identified as a hurricane impacting the region.
Hazards_Annotation: Beneficial rain and wind effects were noted, typical of tropical cyclone remnants.

Time_Annotation: August 1972: Hurricane Diana dissipated a few miles off the Big Island, dropping over 10 inches of rain.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event occurred near the Big Island of Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Diana is classified as a hurricane affecting nearby regions.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rain (over 10 inches) indicates flood hazard in addition to wind effects.

Time_Annotation: September 1972: Hurricane Fernanda may have caused flash flooding near Waipio as it passed to the northeast.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The mention of Waipio places the impact within Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Fernanda is identified as a hurricane.
Hazards_Annotation: Flash flooding is indicated along with storm-related wind hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 1976: Tropical Storm Gwen passed north of Hawaiʻi, dropping 1–2 inches of rain across the state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm impacted the entire state of Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Gwen is recognized as a tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: Light rainfall is the primary reported hazard.

Time_Annotation: July 1978: Hurricane Fico created 15-foot waves, felled trees, and knocked out power across the islands.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The islands of Hawaiʻi were impacted by the storm.
Main_Event_Annotation: Fico is classified as a hurricane in the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: High waves, fallen trees, and power outages indicate wind and flood/surge hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 1982: Hurricane Daniel passed through the islands as a tropical depression causing little damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The passage was over the Hawaiian Islands.
Main_Event_Annotation: Daniel is part of the tropical cyclone system.
Hazards_Annotation: Minimal damage was reported, though typical hazards of wind and light rain are present.

Time_Annotation: November 1982: Hurricane Iwa passed just miles west of Kauai with winds near 50 mph, causing up to $250 million in damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Kauai and other islands in Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Iwa is one of the most damaging hurricanes recorded in Hawaiʻi.
Hazards_Annotation: Severe damage, high wind speeds and heavy rain indicate strong wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: July–August 1983: Hurricane Gil passed over northern Hawaiʻi as a tropical storm.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Northern Hawaiʻi is indicated.
Main_Event_Annotation: Gil is identified as a tropical storm within a hurricane system.
Hazards_Annotation: Minor damage was reported with typical wind and light flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: October 1983: Hurricane Raymond took a path similar to Gil's, but as a depression, causing no damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It affected areas similar to other storms in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Raymond is described as a hurricane in depression form.
Hazards_Annotation: No damage was reported, yet typical hazards remain inherent.

Time_Annotation: July 1985: Hurricane Ignacio, though missing the islands, generated 10 to 15-foot surf damaging coastal roads and structures.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The coastal regions of Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Ignacio is identified as a hurricane impacting coastal conditions.
Hazards_Annotation: Significant surf and minor rainfall indicate coastal hazards primarily due to wind and water surge.

Time_Annotation: July 1986: Waves from Hurricane Estelle caused $2 million in damage and two drownings on Oʻahu.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Oʻahu in Hawaiʻi was directly mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Estelle is classified as a hurricane in the tropical cyclone group.
Hazards_Annotation: Destructive waves and flooding, leading to property damage and loss of life, constitute the hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 1988: Tropical Storm Gilma moved through the islands as a depression, dropping up to 4 inches of heavy rainfall.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm affected the island chain of Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Gilma is identified as a tropical storm in a weaker (depression) phase.
Hazards_Annotation: The locally heavy rainfall reflects flood hazards, with wind being a secondary factor.

Time_Annotation: August 1988: Hurricane Uleki approached Hawaiʻi, with rough surf on Oʻahu causing two drownings.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event specifically affected Oʻahu in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Uleki is classified as a hurricane.
Hazards_Annotation: Rough surf leading to drownings underscores severe wind and water hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 1989: Hurricane Dalili dropped heavy rains—2.33 inches in 24 hours in Honolulu and up to 8 inches near the North Shore.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Honolulu and the North Shore in Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Dalili is categorized as a hurricane impacting rainfall records.
Hazards_Annotation: Record rainfall and heavy downpours denote flood hazards alongside storm winds.

Time_Annotation: August 1991: Hurricane Fefa dissipated shortly before landfall; its gusts reached 58 mph and heavy downpours led to localized flash flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text mentions impacts mainly over Hawaiʻi and Maui.
Main_Event_Annotation: Fefa is classified as a hurricane despite early dissipation.
Hazards_Annotation: Lightning-related injuries, strong surface winds, and flash flooding indicate multiple hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 1992: Hurricane Georgette, observed as a depression, brought squally winds and generated several large waterspouts off Hapuna Beach.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event is noted in the South Kohala district near Hapuna Beach in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Georgette is identified as a hurricane operating in its depression phase.
Hazards_Annotation: Squally winds and waterspout activity represent typical wind and localized flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 1992: Hurricane Iniki struck Kauai as a Category 4 hurricane with winds of up to 140 mph, causing $3.1 billion in damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The island of Kauai in Hawaiʻi was hit directly.
Main_Event_Annotation: Iniki is a major hurricane within the tropical cyclone classification.
Hazards_Annotation: Extreme winds, catastrophic damage, and heavy rainfall confirm severe wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 1992: Hurricane Orlene struck as a tropical depression causing heavy rainfall and road washouts shortly after Iniki.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm’s impact is associated with infrastructural damage in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Orlene is described in its tropical depression phase.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall and subsequent washouts indicate flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 1993: Hurricane Eugene dissipated after dropping valuable rain, causing minor power outages and hazardous traffic conditions.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Various parts of Hawaiʻi were affected as indicated by traffic and power reports.
Main_Event_Annotation: Eugene is part of the tropical cyclone events impacting the islands.
Hazards_Annotation: Rain-induced hazards and power outages denote flood and wind impacts.

Time_Annotation: August 1993: Hurricane Fernanda brought heavy surf up to 15 feet on east-facing beaches from the Big Island to Kauai.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: East-facing beaches on the Big Island and Kauai in Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Fernanda is identified as a hurricane impacting coastal conditions.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy surf and flooding of coastal roads and homes are the primary hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 1994: Tropical Storm Daniel dumped 5 inches of rain over the windward slopes of the Big Island with moderate 6-foot surf along the east and southeast shorelines.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Big Island of Hawaiʻi is specifically mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Daniel is recorded as a tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: Rainfall and moderate surf are indicative of flood and wind hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 1994: Hurricane Emilia passed south of Hawaiʻi, damaging trees and causing 10-foot surf along the Puna and Kau shorelines.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Affected coastal areas in Hawaiʻi such as Puna and Kau.
Main_Event_Annotation: Emilia is identified as a hurricane impacting the region.
Hazards_Annotation: Damage to foliage and coastal surf indicate wind and flooding hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 1994: The remnants of Tropical Storm Fabio brought heavy showers to Big Island and Oahu, with rainfall accumulating to 4 inches.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Big Island and Oahu in Hawaiʻi experienced the rainfall.
Main_Event_Annotation: Fabio is noted in its remnant phase.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy showers leading to moderate rainfall point to flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 1994: Tropical Depression One-C passed just south of the islands, causing severe flooding in Hilo.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Hilo in Hawaiʻi is explicitly mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Even as a tropical depression, it falls under the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Severe flooding in Hilo indicates major flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 1999: Hurricane Dora caused minor wind gusts up to 58 mph on the southern part of the Big Island.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The southern region of the Big Island in Hawaiʻi was affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Dora is classified as a hurricane affecting the region.
Hazards_Annotation: Minor wind gusts are noted, consistent with tropical cyclone hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2000: Hurricane Daniel passed north of the islands, bringing thunderstorms and high surf up to 10 feet on the eastern side of Hawaiʻi.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The eastern side of the island of Hawaiʻi is mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Daniel (2000) is presented as a hurricane in a tropical cyclone context.
Hazards_Annotation: Thunderstorms and high surf indicate wind and flood-related hazards, although damage was minimal.

Time_Annotation: August 2003: Hurricane Jimena passed the Big Island bringing up to 10 inches of rain, 15-foot high surf on windward sections, and a gust of 53 mph at South Point.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Big Island, especially windward sections and South Point, in Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Jimena is recognized as a hurricane within the tropical cyclone family.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall and high surf represent wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2004: The remnants of Hurricane Darby bypassed the islands and, combined with an upper-level trough, dropped up to 5 inches of rain causing flooding and road closures on the Big Island and Oahu.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Affected areas include the Big Island and Oahu in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: The remnants of Darby are counted under tropical cyclones.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rain leading to flooding and road closures indicates significant flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 2005: An upper-level trough with remnants of Hurricane Jova produced unstable conditions and locally heavy rainfall in Hawaiʻi.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The unstable conditions affected the islands of Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Remnants of Jova are included in the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall under unstable conditions signals flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 2005: The remnants of Hurricane Kenneth brought up to 12 inches of rain on the Big Island, with intense rains on Oahu and Kauai causing flash floods.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Big Island, Oahu, and Kauai in Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Kenneth's remnants are part of tropical cyclone events.
Hazards_Annotation: Flash floods and heavy rainfall denote significant flooding hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2007: Hurricane Flossie passed within 100 miles of the Big Island, bringing rain and tropical storm-force winds.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Big Island in Hawaiʻi is mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Flossie is classified as a hurricane affecting the region.
Hazards_Annotation: Tropical storm-force winds and rain indicate typical hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2008: The remnants of Hurricane Hernan brought moisture to the island of Hawaii, causing cloud and shower activity.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The island of Hawaii in the state is mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Remnants of Hernan are included under tropical cyclones.
Hazards_Annotation: The event produced increased moisture and showers, typical though mild tropical cyclone hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2009: The remnants of Hurricane Felicia brought light rainfall to the northern islands.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The northern islands of Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Felicia's remnants are part of the tropical cyclone sequence.
Hazards_Annotation: Light rainfall indicates minimal hazard but falls under the typical pattern.

Time_Annotation: October 2009: Hurricane Nekica struck the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands as a tropical storm.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, part of the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, is noted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Nekica is classified as a hurricane/tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: Minor damage was reported, consistent with the lower-end hazards of tropical storms.

Time_Annotation: December 2010: Tropical Storm Omeka brushed Lisianski Island as a weak tropical storm with no damage reported.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Lisianski Island, part of Hawaiʻi, was affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Omeka is identified as a tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: The weak nature of the storm meant minimal wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 2013: Tropical Storm Flossie passed just north of the Hawaiian Islands before dissipating.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The passage north of Hawaiʻi is noted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Flossie (2013) is recorded as a tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: Minor effects with typical tropical storm wind and light rain conditions.

Time_Annotation: August 2014: Hurricane Iselle made landfall in the southeastern part of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a moderate tropical storm, causing heavy rain, flooding, and minor structural damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The southeastern part of the Island of Hawaiʻi is specified.
Main_Event_Annotation: Iselle is identified as a hurricane/tropical storm in the event.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall, flooding, and structural damage underscore the wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: October 2014: Hurricane Anaski skirted just south of the Hawaiian islands, passing 85 miles southwest of Kauai as a Category 1 hurricane.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It passed near Kauai in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Anaski is recorded as a hurricane operating in the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Limited damage (a few downed trees) indicates relatively mild wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2015: Hurricane Hilda passed within 200 miles southeast of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a tropical depression.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event is referenced in relation to the Island of Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Hilda is classified as a hurricane in its tropical depression stage.
Hazards_Annotation: The report indicates minimal impacts, consistent with low-end atmospheric hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2015: Hurricane Kilo passed well south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a tropical depression, enhancing moisture that led to locally heavy rainfall.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The moisture enhancement affected the vicinity of the Island of Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Kilo is recognized as a hurricane impacting moisture levels.
Hazards_Annotation: Enhanced rainfall from the moisture indicates flood hazards along with tropical cyclone winds.

Time_Annotation: August 2015: Hurricane Loko brushed Pearl and Hermes Atoll as a minimal hurricane with no damage reported.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Pearl and Hermes Atoll are part of the Hawaiian archipelago.
Main_Event_Annotation: Loko is classified under the tropical cyclone group.
Hazards_Annotation: Minimal damage implies that hazards were present but not severe.

Time_Annotation: August–September 2015: Hurricane Ignacio passed about 230 miles northeast of Maui and Molokai as a Category 1 hurricane, causing only minimal impacts.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event is relevant to Maui and Molokai in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Ignacio (2015) is classified as a hurricane in the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Minimal impacts suggest that while wind and flood hazards were present, they were not severe.

Time_Annotation: September 2015: Hurricane Jimena passed well north of the Hawaiian islands before dissipating, bringing scattered heavy rains.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm affected the broader region near Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Jimena (2015) is recognized as a hurricane.
Hazards_Annotation: Scattered heavy rains denote potential flood hazards along with tropical storm winds.

Time_Annotation: September 2015: Tropical Storm Malia brushed Maro Reef as a weak tropical storm.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Maro Reef, part of Hawaiʻi, was brushed by the storm.
Main_Event_Annotation: Malia is classified as a tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: No damage reported, indicating low-level wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 2015: Tropical Storm Niala passed to the southeast of the Big Island, bringing tropical storm force winds and prompting Flood and High Wind Advisories.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Big Island in Hawaiʻi is directly mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Niala is a tropical storm affecting the area.
Hazards_Annotation: Advisories and wind force indicate both wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 2016: Remnants of Hurricane Blas brought showers to Hawaiʻi with peak rainfall between 1 and 2 inches, causing no serious flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The showers impacted areas across Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Blas is included as a tropical cyclone remnant influencing weather.
Hazards_Annotation: Light rainfall indicates minimal flood hazards and low wind impact.

Time_Annotation: July 2016: Remnants of Hurricane Celia generated large swells up to 15 feet on the east-facing shores of Hawaiʻi, causing rough surf that resulted in two drowning deaths on Oahu.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The east-facing shores of Oahu in Hawaiʻi are noted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Celia's remnants are part of the tropical cyclone system affecting the area.
Hazards_Annotation: Strong swells and rough surf, leading to fatalities, illustrate severe wind/wave hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 2016: Hurricane Darby made landfall in southeast Island of Hawaiʻi as a minimal tropical storm bringing heavy rain and widespread flash floods on windward sides.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The southeast Island and windward sides of Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Darby (2016) is classified within tropical cyclones impacting the region.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rain and flash flooding are the primary hazards noted despite overall minor damage.

Time_Annotation: July 2016 (July 31): Remnant moisture from Hurricane Georgette brought heavy rain to Oahu, causing only minor flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Oahu in Hawaiʻi was specifically impacted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Georgette's remnants are included in the tropical cyclone events.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rain leading to minor flooding reflects moderate flood hazard.

Time_Annotation: August 2016: Remnants of Tropical Storm Howard moved across the main Hawaiian Islands on August 7, dropping up to 2 inches of rain with minor flooding in parts of Kauai, Oahu, and Maui.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Kauai, Oahu, and Maui in Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Howard (Remnants) is part of the tropical cyclone classification.
Hazards_Annotation: Minor rainfall and localized flooding align with low-level tropical cyclone hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 2016: Hurricane Madeline passed to the southeast of the Big Island as a weakening tropical storm, producing heavy rain (5–11 inches) and gusty winds.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Big Island of Hawaiʻi experienced the impacts.
Main_Event_Annotation: Madeline is categorized as a tropical storm under the broader cyclone classification.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall and gusty winds denote significant wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 2016: Hurricane Lester passed slowly to the northeast as a Category 1 hurricane with outer rainbands producing heavy showers and minor flooding on the leeward slopes of the Big Island and portions of east Maui.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The impacts were noted on the Big Island and east Maui in Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Lester is recognized as a Category 1 hurricane within the tropical cyclone group.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy showers and minor flooding indicate moderate hazards from wind and water.

Time_Annotation: July 2017: The remnants of Hurricane Fernanda passed to the north of the islands on July 24, producing thunderstorms and heavy showers.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The northern areas of the Hawaiian Islands were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Fernanda’s remnants continue to be classified among tropical cyclones.
Hazards_Annotation: Thunderstorms and heavy showers denote typical hazards of diminished tropical systems.

Time_Annotation: August 2018: Hurricane Hector passed about 200 miles south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a Category 3 hurricane, generating 20-foot high surf and prompting at least 90 rescues off Oahu.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The island of Hawaiʻi and Oahu were particularly affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Hector is a Category 3 hurricane, fitting within the tropical cyclone classification.
Hazards_Annotation: Extremely high surf and dangerous conditions highlight hazardous wind and coastal flooding risks.

Time_Annotation: August 2018: Hurricane Lane slowly approached from the southeast, peaking as a Category 5 hurricane; its outer rainbands caused severe mudslides and flash flooding on the Island of Hawaiʻi with up to 52.02 inches of rain recorded, and one fatality occurred from a river incident.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Island of Hawaiʻi (and its surrounding areas) were heavily impacted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Lane is classified as a major hurricane in the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Severe mudslides, flash flooding, and extreme rainfall illustrate catastrophic wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 2018: Hurricane Norman passed about 300 miles to the northeast of the main Hawaiian islands as a weakening Category 1 hurricane, prompting high surf warnings for eastern shores of Maui and the Island of Hawaiʻi.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Eastern shores of Maui and the Island of Hawaiʻi are mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Norman, though weakening, is part of the tropical cyclone family.
Hazards_Annotation: High surf warnings and associated conditions indicate wind and flood related hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 2018: Hurricane Wala struck the French Frigate Shoals as a Category 3 hurricane, completely destroying the uninhabited East Island in the atoll.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: French Frigate Shoals, including East Island, are part of Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Wala is categorized as a hurricane within the tropical cyclone classification.
Hazards_Annotation: Complete destruction of an island underscores the severe wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 2018: Hurricane Olivia made landfall in northwest Maui as a minimal tropical storm and later again on the northeast coast of Lanai with heavy rains and gusty winds, prompting evacuations.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Northwest Maui and Lanai in Hawaiʻi were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Olivia is noted as a tropical storm making landfall.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rains, gusty winds, and evacuations point to wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 2019: The remnants of Hurricane Barbara passed 120 miles south of Hawaiʻi, producing showers over windward regions and causing power outages for 45,000 customers.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Windward regions of Hawaiʻi, including areas near Maui, were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Barbara's remnants are included in the tropical cyclone classification.
Hazards_Annotation: Showers and power outages indicate hazards related to wind and minor flooding.

Time_Annotation: August 2019: Hurricane Erick passed about 230 miles south of the island of Hawaiʻi as a tropical storm, bringing swells and rainfall.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The island of Hawaiʻi was influenced by Erick’s passage.
Main_Event_Annotation: Erick is identified as a tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: Swells and rainfall are indicative of typical tropical cyclone hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2019: Subsequently, Hurricane Flossie approached Hawaiʻi as a weakening tropical depression before passing northeast of the Big Island.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The area northeast of the Big Island in Hawaiʻi was affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Flossie (2019) is categorized as a tropical depression within the cyclone classification.
Hazards_Annotation: Minimal effects were noted, though the system is still associated with typical tropical hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 2020: Hurricane Douglas passed just north of the Hawaiian Islands, bringing heavy rainfall and gusty winds, and was the closest hurricane to Oahu on record.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The entire Hawaiian Islands, with Oahu noted specifically, were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Douglas is a hurricane part of the tropical cyclone family.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall and gusty winds are reflective of common tropical cyclone hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 2021: The remnants of Hurricane Linda traversed the Hawaiian Islands, bringing heavy rain and gusty winds with minor damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The remnants affected multiple areas across Hawaiʻi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Linda’s remnants fall under tropical cyclone classifications.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rain and gusty winds characterize the hazards, though overall damage was minor.

Time_Annotation: July 2022: Hurricane Darby bypassed to the south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a weakening tropical storm, bringing rain and high surf with only minor damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Island of Hawaiʻi is specifically referenced.
Main_Event_Annotation: Darby (2022) is tracked as a tropical storm in the cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Rain, high surf, and minimal damage indicate modest wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 2023: Hurricane Calvin passed to the south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a tropical storm, bringing heavy rainfall and gusty winds with no significant damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Island of Hawaiʻi is mentioned as being near the storm.
Main_Event_Annotation: Calvin is classified as a tropical storm within the cyclone group.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rains and gusty winds denote the typical hazards, though impacts were minimal.

Time_Annotation: August 2023: Hurricane Dora passed far to the south of the Island of Hawaiʻi; however, a steep pressure gradient between a strong northern anticyclone and Dora produced extremely strong winds over the islands, contributing to multiple wildfires on Hawaiʻi and Maui.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The islands of Hawaiʻi and Maui were affected by the extreme winds.
Main_Event_Annotation: Dora (2023) is recognized as a hurricane affecting conditions indirectly.
Hazards_Annotation: Incredible gradient winds and consequent wildfires illustrate severe wind hazards and secondary flood concerns.

Time_Annotation: August 2024: Hurricane Hone passed just south of the Island of Hawaiʻi while strengthening as a Category 1 hurricane, bringing heavy rains, strong winds, and life-threatening surf and rip currents.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Island of Hawaiʻi was directly affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Hone is classified as a hurricane in the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: The combination of heavy rain, strong winds, and dangerous surf/rip currents represent significant hazards.

Main_Event_Annotation: Event identified as Tropical Storm Dolly (Outer Rainbands).
Hazards_Annotation: Urban flooding and relief from drought conditions are highlighted.

Time_Annotation: September 20, 2014 – Remnants of Hurricane Odile cause flooding in Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The flooding in Austin, Texas is noted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event recorded as the remnants of Hurricane Odile.
Hazards_Annotation: Flooding that resulted in a fatality (sheriff's deputy) is emphasized.

Time_Annotation: Mid-June 2015 – Tropical Storm Bill makes landfall on Matagorda Island.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Areas including Matagorda, Palacios, Port O'Connor, Port Lavaca, and Wharton in Texas experienced impacts.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event designated as Tropical Storm Bill (2015).
Hazards_Annotation: Gusty winds, storm surge and heavy rainfall leading to significant flood hazards are noted.

Time_Annotation: October 20–24, 2015 – The remnants of Hurricane Patricia bring heavy rain to Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Corsicana and the Interstate 45 corridor in Texas were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Attributed to the remnants of Hurricane Patricia.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall causing floods and highway closures is noted.

Time_Annotation: September 8, 2016 – The remnants of Hurricane Newton bring heavy rains to parts of western Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Western Texas experienced rainfall from the remnant system.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event recorded as the remnants of Hurricane Newton.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rains are noted without significant damage reports.

Time_Annotation: June 22, 2017 – Tropical Storm Cindy makes landfall near Port Arthur.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Impacts were noted on Port Arthur and the Bolivar Peninsula in Texas.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event designated as Tropical Storm Cindy.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind effects causing a fatality and flooding are highlighted.

Time_Annotation: August 25, 2017 – Hurricane Harvey makes landfall on San José Island near Rockport.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Extensive impacts across Southeast Texas, including Houston and Rockport, are recorded.
Main_Event_Annotation: Classified as Hurricane Harvey.
Hazards_Annotation: Record-setting rainfall, catastrophic flooding, and widespread wind damage are reported.

Time_Annotation: September 17–19, 2019 – Tropical Storm Imelda makes landfall near Freeport, Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern Texas, including Jefferson County, experienced catastrophic flooding.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event recorded as Tropical Storm Imelda.
Hazards_Annotation: A peak rainfall of 43.39 inches and widespread flooding resulting in fatalities are noted.

Time_Annotation: July 25, 2020 – Hurricane Hanna makes landfall roughly 12 mi north-northwest of Port Mansfield.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm impacted the Rio Grande Valley, Hidalgo and Cameron counties in Texas.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Hanna.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall, flash floods, widespread power outages, and crop damages are reported.

Time_Annotation: August 26, 2020 – The western extent of Hurricane Laura impacts southeast Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeast Texas, notably Orange County, suffered major power outages and wind impacts.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event recorded as Hurricane Laura.
Hazards_Annotation: High wind gusts, power outages, and carbon monoxide poisoning incidents are emphasized.

Time_Annotation: Mid-September 2020 – Tropical Storm Beta brings extensive rainfall across southeast Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Areas in and around Houston, including Brooks, Texas are affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event designated as Tropical Storm Beta.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rains causing significant flooding and damage to homes are noted.

Time_Annotation: October 9, 2020 – Hurricane Delta makes landfall near Creole, Louisiana, affecting Southeast Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeast Texas and coastal areas experienced impacts including beach erosion.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Delta.
Hazards_Annotation: Hurricane-force winds, 5–10 inches of rain, and coastal flooding are reported.

Time_Annotation: September 14, 2021 – Hurricane Nicholas makes landfall on the eastern part of Matagorda Peninsula.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Affected areas include Brazoria and Matagorda counties, with significant damage in Surfside Beach.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event recorded as Hurricane Nicholas.
Hazards_Annotation: High winds, widespread power outages, and heavy rainfall are documented.

Time_Annotation: August 22, 2023 – Tropical Storm Harold makes landfall on Padre Island.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Impacted Padre Island, Loyola Beach, Corpus Christi, and Mustang Island in Texas.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event designated as Tropical Storm Harold.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind gusts up to 67 mph and approximately 7 inches of rainfall led to power outages and flooding.

Time_Annotation: June 19–20, 2024 – Tropical Storm Alberto makes landfall in Tamaulipas, Mexico, bringing heavy rains to the Texas Gulf Coast.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Impacted the Texas Gulf Coast and Tamaulipas with a fatal rip current in Galveston.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event recorded as Tropical Storm Alberto.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rains and resultant flooding along with rip current hazards are reported.

Time_Annotation: July 8, 2024 – Hurricane Beryl makes landfall near Matagorda as a Category 1 hurricane.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm significantly affected Matagorda, the Houston area, and Freeport in Texas.
Main_Event_Annotation: Event designated as Hurricane Beryl.
Hazards_Annotation: Strong winds, coastal and urban flooding, extensive power outages, and fatalities due to high temperatures post-storm are noted.

Time_Annotation: September 9, 2000 – Tropical Depression Nine makes landfall near the Texas and Louisiana border as a tropical depression with winds of 30 mph (48 km/h).
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It made landfall near the Texas and Louisiana border with most rain affecting Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Depression Nine, a type of tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: The report mentions 30 mph winds, a storm surge peaking at 3 ft, and damage from strong thunderstorm winds indicative of wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: Early–June 2001 – Tropical Storm Allison makes landfall near Freeport, Texas on June 5 and then a second landfall on Morgan City on June 11.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm hit near Freeport, Texas and Morgan City in Louisiana, causing catastrophic flooding across Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Allison, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: It produced high winds, catastrophic flooding, and even tornado damage in Zachary.

Time_Annotation: August 6, 2001 – Tropical Storm Barry causes tides of 2–3 ft along the southeastern coast of Louisiana before making landfall on Santa Rosa Beach, Florida.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The system produced effects along the southeastern Louisiana coast and then made landfall in Florida.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Barry, which is a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: Tidal surges and tropical storm winds indicate hazards from both wind and flooding.

Time_Annotation: August 5, 2002 – Tropical Storm Bertha makes landfall on Boothville and moves across Louisiana before moving back into the Gulf of Mexico on August 7.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm impacted Boothville, Slidell, and St. Tammany Parish in Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Bertha, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The heavy rainfall and flash flooding along with moderate winds indicate both wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 5, 2002 – Tropical Storm Fay develops offshore the Louisiana coast before making landfall in Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Its development offshore Louisiana and subsequent landfall in Texas (with warnings issued for Louisiana) show its impact on both areas.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Fay, part of the tropical cyclone family.
Hazards_Annotation: Storm surge causing coastal flooding highlights both wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 14, 2002 – Tropical Storm Hanna makes landfall near the mouth of the Mississippi River and then on the Alabama–Mississippi border.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Although making landfall near Louisiana, the storm also affected parts of Alabama and Mississippi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Hanna, a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: Moderate winds (around 50 mph) are noted, with minimal flooding effects reported.

Time_Annotation: September 26, 2002 – Hurricane Isidore makes landfall just west of Grand Isle as a Tropical Storm.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It affected regions in Louisiana including Metarie and Terrebonne Parish.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Isidore, part of the tropical cyclone sequence (weakened to a tropical storm at landfall).
Hazards_Annotation: Winds and widespread rainfall causing drainage failures and street flooding signal both hazards.

Time_Annotation: October 3, 2002 – Hurricane Lily makes landfall near Intracoastal City as a weakening Category 1 hurricane.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It struck near Intracoastal City in Louisiana, affecting coastal regions.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Lily, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind gusts up to 120 mph combined with heavy rainfall and storm surge indicate significant wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: June 30, 2003 – Tropical Storm Bill brought a moderate storm surge peaking at 5.8 ft at several locations in Louisiana.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It impacted areas including Chauvin, Montegut, and St. Tammany Parish in Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Bill, which is a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: The storm surge flooding roads and homes along with rough waves indicate both wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 31, 2003 – Tropical Storm Grace drops light rainfall across the state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The effects were observed across Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Grace, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Only light rainfall was reported, indicating minimal wind-related effects with little flooding.

Time_Annotation: September 15–16 and September 22–23, 2004 – Around the time of Hurricane Ivan's initial landfall, impactful weather was observed in Louisiana.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Impacts were noted in Plaquemines and St. Bernard Parishes in Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Ivan, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind gusts up to 100 mph and storm surge flooding are described.

Time_Annotation: October 10, 2004 – Tropical Storm Matthew caused a storm surge and significant rainfall across parts of Louisiana.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Regions including Frenier, Grand Isle, Terrebonne Parish, Lafouche Parish, and LaPlace in Louisiana were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Matthew, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The combination of storm surge, heavy rainfall, and flooding of homes and roads indicate both hazard types.

Time_Annotation: July 5, 2005 – Hurricane Cindy brought wind gusts of 70 mph to New Orleans.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event notably affected New Orleans in Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Cindy, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Strong winds led to tree damage and power outages, with some street flooding also reported.

Time_Annotation: July 10, 2005 – Hurricane Dennis produced light precipitation and a wind gust of 47 mph at Lakefront Airport in New Orleans.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: New Orleans, Louisiana was affected by its light precipitation and wind.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Dennis, a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: Mild wind gusts are noted with light precipitation and minimal flooding.

Time_Annotation: August 29, 2005 – Hurricane Katrina’s eye made landfall, leading to massive flooding in New Orleans.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Widespread damage was observed in New Orleans and multiple parishes in Louisiana, with impacts also in Mississippi.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Katrina, one of the most significant tropical cyclones in U.S. history.
Hazards_Annotation: Levee failures, destructive winds, and catastrophic flooding are emphasized.

Time_Annotation: September 24, 2005 – Hurricane Rita made landfall as a Category 3 hurricane on the Texas-Louisiana border.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It impacted coastal communities in Cameron Parish, Louisiana and areas along the Texas-Louisiana border.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Rita, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Devastating storm surge and coastal flooding combined with high winds are noted.

Time_Annotation: September 13, 2007 – Hurricane Humbert passed through the state as a weakening tropical storm after making landfall at High Island, Texas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event influenced Texas at landfall and had subsequent impacts across Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Humbert, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Moderate wind conditions were observed with limited additional impacts.

Time_Annotation: September 22, 2007 – Tropical Depression Ten was the first tropical cyclone to directly threaten New Orleans since Katrina.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It directly threatened New Orleans in Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Depression Ten, a member of the tropical cyclone family.
Hazards_Annotation: Only limited wind effects were reported with generally minimal impacts.

Time_Annotation: August 4, 2008 – Tropical Storm Edouard made landfall near Gilchrist, Texas with tropical storm force winds affecting southwest Louisiana.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The system affected southwest Louisiana and nearby regions in Texas.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Edouard, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Tropical storm force winds were noted with limited additional hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 1, 2008 – Hurricane Gustav reached the Louisiana coast on the morning of September 1, making landfall near Cocodrie as a Category 2 hurricane.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The hurricane affected 34 parishes in Louisiana with significant damage.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Gustav, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Sustained tropical storm-force winds and heavy rainfall led to widespread flooding and structural damage.

Time_Annotation: September 13, 2008 – Hurricane Ike made landfall on Galveston Island, Texas and produced significant storm surge across the southwest Louisiana coast.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It impacted both Galveston, Texas and the southwestern coastline of Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Ike, a major tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Significant storm surge and damaging winds were reported, leading to hazardous coastal conditions.

Time_Annotation: November 10, 2009 – Hurricane Ida passed by the southeast Louisiana coast as a weakening tropical storm.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The system affected the southeast coast of Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Ida, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Weakened wind conditions were reported with light precipitation.

Time_Annotation: July 25–26, 2010 – The remnants of Tropical Storm Bonnie produced a heavy rain event in West Baton Rouge Parish.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The rainfall and flooding impacted West Baton Rouge Parish in Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the remnants of Tropical Storm Bonnie, part of tropical cyclone activity.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall leading to flooding along with moderate winds are cited as hazards.

Time_Annotation: Mid–August 2010 – The remnants of Tropical Depression Five made two separate landfalls within the state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Multiple landfalls and flood watches were issued in Louisiana, including Avoyelles Parish.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Depression Five, which is part of the tropical cyclone family.
Hazards_Annotation: Intense rain and thunderstorms led to flooding and associated wind effects.

Time_Annotation: September 4, 2011 – Tropical Storm Lee led to torrential rainfall and a four‐foot storm surge in New Orleans.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: New Orleans, Natchitoches Parish, and Slidell in Louisiana experienced significant impacts.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Lee, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall, storm surge, and even a related fire indicate both wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: June 23–24, 2012 – Tropical Storm Debby prompted a state of emergency with associated storm surge.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern areas of Louisiana, including Shell Beach, were impacted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Debby, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Onshore flow led to storm surge and flooding, combining wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 29, 2012 – Hurricane Isaac came ashore as a large Category 1 hurricane, producing an eleven‐foot storm surge.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It significantly impacted areas like Grand Isle and LaPlace in Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Isaac, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Hurricane-force winds and massive flooding (with rescue operations) indicate both hazards.

Time_Annotation: October 6, 2013 – A state of emergency was declared ahead of Tropical Storm Karen, which dissipated with negligible effects.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Louisiana experienced only minimal rainfall as impacts were negligible.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Karen, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The event had minimal wind and rain effects, resulting in limited hazards.

Time_Annotation: June 22, 2017 – Tropical Storm Cindy made landfall in extreme southwest Louisiana near Sabine Pass.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm affected extreme southwest Louisiana near Sabine Pass.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Cindy, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Maximum sustained winds of 50 mph were recorded, highlighting wind as the primary hazard.

Time_Annotation: August 30, 2017 – Hurricane Harvey made its third and final U.S. landfall at Sabine Pass as a weakened tropical storm.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It affected southwest Louisiana and areas along the Texas-Louisiana border near Sabine Pass.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Harvey, part of the tropical cyclone sequence.
Hazards_Annotation: Significant flooding across southwest Louisiana followed landfall, combined with wind effects.

Time_Annotation: October 8, 2017 – Hurricane Nate made landfall in the Mississippi River delta with 85 mph winds.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The Mississippi River delta in Louisiana was affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Nate, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The reported 85 mph winds indicate wind as the primary hazard.

Time_Annotation: July 13, 2019 – Hurricane Barry made landfall at Marsh Island and near Intracoastal City as a minimal Category 1 hurricane.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: It affected Marsh Island, Intracoastal City, and caused flooding in New Orleans and Plaquemines Parish.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Barry, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall, mandatory evacuations, and flooding emphasize both wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: October 26, 2019 – The remnants of Tropical Storm Olga produced 10–15 in of rainfall throughout Southeastern Louisiana.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern Louisiana experienced heavy rainfall.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the remnants of Tropical Storm Olga, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The exceptionally high rainfall amounts led predominantly to flooding.

Time_Annotation: June 7, 2020 – Tropical Storm Cristobal made landfall east of Grand Isle with a storm surge reaching 5 ft.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Areas east of Grand Isle in Louisiana were impacted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Cristobal, part of the tropical cyclone system.
Hazards_Annotation: The combination of storm surge and heavy rainfall signifies both wind and flooding hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 24, 2020 – Hurricane Marco passed just south of the Mississippi River delta as a weak tropical storm.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Regions near the Mississippi River delta in Louisiana were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Marco, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Weak tropical storm conditions with minimal wind and flooding effects were observed.

Time_Annotation: August 27, 2020 – Hurricane Laura made landfall near the Louisiana–Texas border as a high‐end Category 4 hurricane.

Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Laura, a major tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Catastrophic wind damage coupled with a storm surge as high as 17 ft led to widespread flooding and destruction.

Time_Annotation: October 9, 2020 – Hurricane Delta made landfall 15 miles east of where Laura did as a Category 2 hurricane.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Coastal regions in Louisiana experienced further impacts following Laura.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Delta, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Strong winds and additional flooding hampered ongoing recovery efforts from Laura.

Time_Annotation: October 28, 2020 – Hurricane Zeta made landfall near Cocodrie, Louisiana as a Category 3 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm’s eye passed directly over New Orleans and surrounding areas in Louisiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Zeta, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: High winds and extensive flooding effects are highlighted in the report.

Time_Annotation: June 19, 2021 – Tropical Storm Claudette formed near Houma, Louisiana, bringing gusty winds and heavy rainfall.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm affected areas in southeastern Louisiana near Houma.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Claudette, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Gusty winds coupled with heavy rainfall indicate both wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 29, 2021 – Hurricane Ida made landfall at Port Fourchon, Louisiana as a high‐end Category 4 hurricane.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Port Fourchon and surrounding regions in Louisiana were severely impacted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Ida, a major tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Catastrophic wind damage and extensive flooding, with 33 fatalities, are reported as major hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 8, 2024 – Hurricane Beryl made its first landfall in Texas and then its second landfall near Intracoastal City in Louisiana, bringing tropical storm‐force conditions.

Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Beryl, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rainfall, power outages, and tornado activity associated with Beryl highlight wind and flood hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 11, 2024 – Hurricane Francine made landfall at peak intensity in Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana as a Category 2 hurricane.

Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Francine, part of the tropical cyclone family.

Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Locations such as Adjuntas and Maricao were notably affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: A second report identifies this as Tropical Storm Erika.
Hazards_Annotation: Tropical storm-force winds disrupted the power grid, leaving approximately 250,000 people without electricity.

Time_Annotation: September 6–7 - Hurricane Irma passed north of Puerto Rico, producing sustained tropical storm force winds and heavy rainfall.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The main island and Culebra experienced significant impacts.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Irma.
Hazards_Annotation: Strong winds and heavy rainfall led to loss of essential services and widespread damage.

Time_Annotation: September 20–21 - Hurricane Maria made landfall near Yabucoa, causing catastrophic damage.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The devastation impacted Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Maria.
Hazards_Annotation: Catastrophic winds and flooding resulted in widespread infrastructure collapse and power failures.

Time_Annotation: July 9–10 - Hurricane Beryl dropped over 8 inches of rain, triggering flash flooding and a landslide in Naranjito.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Impacts were observed in Naranjito and near Humacao.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Beryl.
Hazards_Annotation: Flash flooding and inundated roadways were significant hazard indicators.

Time_Annotation: August 28–29 - Hurricane Dorian moved farther northeast than anticipated, resulting in very limited effects in Puerto Rico.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: A minor impact was noted in Bayamón, with one indirect fatality reported.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Dorian.
Hazards_Annotation: Effects were minimal, with only an indirect fatality occurring.

Time_Annotation: September 24–25 - Tropical Storm Karen dropped a peak of 5 inches of rain in Coamo, sweeping away a bridge and causing widespread flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Multiple municipalities including Coamo, Utuado, Jayuya, Yabucoa, Aguadilla, Aibonito, and Toa Baja were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Karen.
Hazards_Annotation: The event led to flooded roads, mudslides, and washed-away infrastructure.

Time_Annotation: July 30–31 - Hurricane Isaias caused extensive power and water service outages in Puerto Rico.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Significant impacts were recorded in regions including Jayuya.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Isaias.
Hazards_Annotation: High winds contributed to widespread infrastructural damage and outages.

Time_Annotation: August 22–23 - Tropical Storm Laura downed trees and caused flooding in Salinas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Areas including Salinas and Villalba were impacted.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Laura.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind gusts downed trees while heavy rains led to flooding and power outages.

Time_Annotation: September 18 (indirect) - Hurricane Teddy generated rip currents and churning waves off La Pocita Beach, leading to drownings.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The incident occurred off La Pocita Beach in Loíza, Puerto Rico.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Teddy.
Hazards_Annotation: Rip currents and churning waves created hazardous conditions leading to fatalities.

Time_Annotation: August 11 - Tropical Storm Fred generated a 55 km/h (34 mph) wind gust in Lajas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The wind gust was recorded in Lajas, Puerto Rico.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Fred.
Hazards_Annotation: The primary hazard was a notable wind gust of 55 km/h.

Time_Annotation: September (indirectly) - Hurricane Larry generated rough surf and rip currents that led to a drowning in Puerto Rico.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Coastal areas in Puerto Rico were affected by rough surf conditions.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Larry.
Hazards_Annotation: Rough surf and rip currents created hazardous conditions resulting in a fatality.

Time_Annotation: September 21 - Tropical Storm Peter brought heavy rain showers that led to mudslides and minor flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Towns such as Lares, Morovis, Carolina, Corozal, Utuado, and Vega Baja experienced impacts.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Peter.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rains resulted in mudslides and localized flooding.

Time_Annotation: September 4–5 - The outer bands of Hurricane Earl produced 3 to 5 inches of rainfall, with a peak of 7.7 inches near Finca La Loma, and lightning strikes led to fatalities.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Eastern Puerto Rico, particularly near Salinas, was affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Earl.
Hazards_Annotation: Fatal lightning strikes were reported, marking the primary hazard for this event.

Time_Annotation: September 18–19 - Hurricane Fiona caused widespread power outages, heavy rainfall, and destructive winds across Puerto Rico.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Impacts were observed island-wide, notably near Ponce.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Fiona.
Hazards_Annotation: Torrential rains, strong winds, landslides, and washed-away bridges characterized the hazard profile.

Time_Annotation: November 4–6 - Hurricane Nicole brought torrential rains of 4–8 inches to Puerto Rico.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The entire island experienced the heavy rainfall.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Nicole.
Hazards_Annotation: Torrential rains prompted flooding conditions across the territory.

Time_Annotation: August 22-24 - Tropical Storm Franklin affected Puerto Rico.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm’s impact was noted across Puerto Rico.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Storm Franklin.
Hazards_Annotation: No specific hazard details beyond the storm’s general effects were provided.

Time_Annotation: September 10–11, 1900 — The extratropical remnants of the 1900 Galveston hurricane quickly traverse the state before entering Lake Michigan at Milwaukee.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm traversed the state—with data from northern and central Wisconsin—and affected areas near Milwaukee along Lake Michigan.
Main_Event_Annotation: Described as the extratropical remnants of the 1900 Galveston hurricane.
Hazards_Annotation: Rainfall amounts peaked at 4.25 in with many stations recording over 1 in, suggesting a risk of flood conditions.

Time_Annotation: June 14, 1906 — The remnants of a tropical storm produce light rain across southeastern parts of the state; accumulations reach 0.4–0.5 in.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Light rain was reported across southeastern parts of the state (Wisconsin).
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the remnants of a tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: Only light rainfall (0.4–0.5 in) was observed with no significant hazardous impact.

Time_Annotation: October 19–20, 1916 — The remnants of a hurricane produce rainfall across the state, reaching 1.5–2 in in southeastern counties.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Rainfall was produced across the state, notably in southeastern counties of Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Referred to as the remnants of a hurricane, implying an extratropical transition.
Hazards_Annotation: While measurable rainfall (1.5–2 in) was recorded, no explicit hazardous effects were mentioned.

Time_Annotation: June 26, 1921 — It brought less than 0.75 inches to the entire state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precipitation affected the entire state of Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Inferred as part of the tropical cyclone events affecting Wisconsin.
Hazards_Annotation: With less than 0.75 inches of rain reported, no hazardous conditions were described.

Time_Annotation: October 17-18-19, 1923 — It dropped over 2 inches precipitation to southeastern Wisconsin.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precipitation was concentrated in southeastern Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Inferred from context as a tropical cyclone remnant event.
Hazards_Annotation: Despite over 2 inches of rain falling, no explicit hazardous impacts were noted.

Time_Annotation: September 24–25, 1941 — The entire state received precipitation with the southeast corner of the state recording up to 1.5 inches.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precipitation affected all of Wisconsin, with the southeast corner noted specifically.
Main_Event_Annotation: Assumed as part of the series of tropical cyclone events impacting the state.
Hazards_Annotation: The report only noted rainfall without mentioning any associated hazards.

Time_Annotation: October 1949 Texas hurricane — Extratropical remnants of the Category 2 hurricane traversed the state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The extratropical remnants traversed the state of Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Explicitly described as extratropical remnants of a Category 2 hurricane.
Hazards_Annotation: No specific hazardous conditions were detailed beyond the storm’s passage.

Time_Annotation: 1960 Texas tropical storm — Peak rainfall of 2.83 in at the Eau Pleine Reservoir.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event impacted areas such as the Eau Pleine Reservoir in Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as a Texas tropical storm impacting Wisconsin.
Hazards_Annotation: Only peak rainfall was noted without mention of additional hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 12–14, 1961 — The extratropical remnants of Hurricane Carla brought 54 hours of rainfall to much of the Upper Midwest, with creeks and rivers overtopping their banks and highways experiencing flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Areas such as Brodhead in Wisconsin experienced flooding due to overtopped banks.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the extratropical remnants of Hurricane Carla.
Hazards_Annotation: Flooding on highways and overtopped creeks indicate a clear flood hazard.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: One person was injured when a wall collapsed in Janesville.

Time_Annotation: June 26, 1968 — Rains from Tropical Storm Candy fell across much of Wisconsin, with heavy rains elevating streams and high winds downing power lines.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Central Appleton, Milwaukee, and other parts of Wisconsin were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Directly identified as Tropical Storm Candy.
Hazards_Annotation: Reports of flooding basements and elevated streams coupled with high winds causing power outages confirm both flood and wind hazards.

Time_Annotation: August 21, 1983 – The remnants of Hurricane Alicia combined with a warm front to produce widespread rainfall and moderate winds.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Northeastern Wisconsin, including areas near Green Bay, Milwaukee, and Kenosha, were noted.
Main_Event_Annotation: The event is identified as the remnants of Hurricane Alicia.
Hazards_Annotation: Damaging winds (up to 38 mph and downing trees and power lines) were highlighted.

Time_Annotation: Hurricane Juan1985 — Peak rainfall of 4.9 in in Marinette.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Marinette in Wisconsin experienced significant rainfall.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Juan, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The report only mentions peak rainfall without detailing additional hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 24–26, 1986 — The remnants of Eastern Pacific Hurricane Newton brought heavy rain that exacerbated flooding, along with severe thunderstorms and downbursts.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southern portions of Wisconsin, including Beloit, Kenosha County, and Sheboygan, were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Attributed to the remnants of Hurricane Newton.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rain led to flooding while downbursts and severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds.

Time_Annotation: September 20–21, 1988 — The extratropical remnants of Hurricane Gilbert crossed southeastern Wisconsin with rainfall not exceeding 1 in.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern Wisconsin was the primary area mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Referred to as the extratropical remnants of Hurricane Gilbert.
Hazards_Annotation: Rainfall was light (not exceeding 1 in), and no hazardous effects were described.

Time_Annotation: August 4, 1989 — Following the dissipation of Hurricane Chantal's surface circulation, its remnant cloud shield produced significant precipitation accompanied by severe thunderstorms, damaging winds, and hail.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Regions such as Port Washington, La Crosse, and Janesville in Wisconsin were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the remnants of Hurricane Chantal after its surface circulation dissipated.
Hazards_Annotation: Damaging winds (up to 75 mph) and hail up to 2.25 in in diameter were reported, leading to structural and tree damage.

Time_Annotation: September 25–27, 1992 — Dual rain events from the remnants of Pacific Hurricane Lester affected the entire state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The entire state of Wisconsin was subject to the rainfall events.
Main_Event_Annotation: Linked to the remnants of Hurricane Lester.
Hazards_Annotation: Only rainfall was noted without further hazardous conditions.

Time_Annotation: September 14–15, 1998 — Light to moderate rain accompanied the extratropical remnant of Tropical Storm Frances.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Darlington in Wisconsin was specifically mentioned for rainfall accumulations.
Main_Event_Annotation: Characterized as the extratropical remnant of Tropical Storm Frances.
Hazards_Annotation: The event reported only light to moderate rain without further hazardous impacts.

Time_Annotation: July 16–17, 2005 — The slow-moving remnants of Hurricane Dennis brought very light rain to parts of Wisconsin amid ongoing drought conditions.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Affected areas include parts of Wisconsin such as Phelps.
Main_Event_Annotation: Attributed to the remnants of Hurricane Dennis.
Hazards_Annotation: Very light rain was recorded, and despite the backdrop of drought, no additional hazards were described.

Time_Annotation: September 4–5, 2008 — Heavy rains accompanied the passage of former Hurricane Gustav, with accumulations reaching 3.14 in and localized ponding affecting roads.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Particularly, Kenosha in southeastern Wisconsin experienced these conditions.
Main_Event_Annotation: Referred to as the passage of former Hurricane Gustav.
Hazards_Annotation: Localized ponding and the potential for flooding in low-lying areas were noted.

Time_Annotation: September 15, 2008 — Light rainfall occurred in far southeastern parts of the state with the passage of former Hurricane Ike.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Far southeastern areas of Wisconsin, including Kenosha, were mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: The event was associated with the passage of former Hurricane Ike.
Hazards_Annotation: Only light rainfall was reported without any significant hazardous outcomes.

Time_Annotation: September 2–3, 2012 — The remnants of Hurricane Isaac brought negligible rainfall to extreme southeastern Wisconsin, failing to alleviate drought conditions.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Extreme southeastern Wisconsin is noted as the affected region.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the remnants of Hurricane Isaac.
Hazards_Annotation: Negligible rainfall was observed, with no hazardous effects described.

Time_Annotation: October 30–31, 2012 — A tight pressure gradient between the remnants of Hurricane Sandy and a high-pressure area produced gusty winds and minor beach erosion along Lake Michigan’s coast.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Coastal areas along Lake Michigan from Sheboygan to Kenosha in Wisconsin were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: The event was driven by the remnants of Hurricane Sandy.
Hazards_Annotation: Gusty winds—with sustained speeds of 25–30 mph and gusts up to 55 mph—were reported, causing minor beach erosion.

Time_Annotation: May 30–31, 2018 — As a tropical cyclone progressing unusually far inland, Tropical Depression Alberto brought light rainfall to the eastern side.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event impacted regions in Wisconsin as the system progressed inland.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Depression Alberto, part of the tropical cyclone family.
Hazards_Annotation: Only light rainfall was reported, with no additional hazardous conditions noted.

Time_Annotation: October 26–27, 2019 — The fast-moving extratropical remnant of Tropical Storm Olga brought light rainfall as it traversed Lake Michigan.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern Wisconsin, particularly near Kenosha, experienced the effects of the system.
Main_Event_Annotation: Noted as the extratropical remnant of Tropical Storm Olga.
Hazards_Annotation: The report only mentions light rainfall without significant hazardous impacts.

Time_Annotation: June 9–10, 2020 — The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal traversed the state, with widespread rainfall, record wind gusts, and isolated flash flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: West‐central Wisconsin, including areas near Madison and Augusta, were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system transitioned into an extratropical cyclone as it impacted Wisconsin.
Hazards_Annotation: Isolated flash flooding and wind gusts (up to 51 mph) were reported, indicating both flood and wind hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 9, 2024 - The remnants of Hurricane Beryl brought rainfall in Southeastern Wisconsin.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern Wisconsin is noted as the primary affected region.
Main_Event_Annotation: Attributed to the remnants of Hurricane Beryl.
Hazards_Annotation: The report mentions rainfall only, without additional hazardous details.

Time_Annotation: April 1, 2023: A strong cold front spawned seven tornadoes across the state, tying the November 1989 tornado outbreak for the most New Jersey twisters in a single day. These included three EF2 tornadoes, the first of which touched down in Jackson Township; it snapped dozens of trees and wrecked a newly-built warehouse. Another EF2 hit the same township just six minutes after the previous one dissipated, which was strong enough to destroy a roof. In Sea Girt, an EF2 tornado lifted a roof and moved it 750 ft (230 m). There were also EF1 tornadoes in Cinnaminson, Crosswicks, Allentown, and Mays Landing.[94][95]

Event_Names: 2002 Tornado in St. Clair County, Kenner, Galatia, and Dongola Region
Time_Annotation: April 27, 2002– A brief F1 tornado touched down in St. Clair County and Kenner; an F2 tornado tracked through Galatia; a long-tracked intense tornado moved across Union and Johnson counties in Dongola, with additional F2 in Ganntown and an F3 in Pope County.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Locations include St. Clair, Kenner, Galatia, Union, Johnson, Dongola, Ganntown, and Pope County.
Main_Event_Annotation: Multiple tornado intensities (F1, F2, F3) confirm the event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage from the tornadoes is the primary hazard.

Event_Names: 2003 Tornado in Kentucky and Massac County
Time_Annotation: May 4, 2003– An F1 tornado touched down in Kentucky before crossing into Massac County, downing power lines and damaging trailers; twin tornadoes in Pope County produced F1-leveled tree damage before briefly crossing into Kentucky.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Affected areas are Kentucky, Massac County, and Pope County.
Main_Event_Annotation: F1 tornado events characterize this occurrence.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind hazards are associated with these F1 tornadoes.

Event_Names: 2003 Tornado in Monroe, Pulaski, Massac, and Alexander Counties
Time_Annotation: May 6, 2003– Multiple tornadoes were reported: an F1 tornado in Monroe County, an F1 east of Red Bud, brief F0 tornadoes in Walsh and near Miller City, a violent F4 tornado tracked 33 miles across Pulaski, Massac and Pope counties, an F0 in Cypress, an F2 in Alexander County crossing into Missouri, and additional brief F0 events in Johnson and Massac counties, with an F2 near Metropolis.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The description covers a broad region including Monroe, Red Bud, Walsh, Miller City, Pulaski, Massac, Pope, Cypress, Alexander, Johnson counties, and near Metropolis.
Main_Event_Annotation: The mix of F1, violent F4, F0, and F2 tornadoes indicates a complex tornado event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage is the primary hazard across the multiple tornado reports.

Time_Annotation: May 8, 2003– A brief F0 tornado touched down west of Staunton and another F0 tornado touched down south of Oskaloosa.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event mentions locations near Staunton and Oskaloosa.
Main_Event_Annotation: The F0 ratings designate these as tornado events, albeit minor.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind, though less intense, is the hazard in these events.

Time_Annotation: May 9, 2003– A tornado inflicted F0-leveled damage to multiple homes and blew over a semi-truck in Sangamon County.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event is noted in Sangamon County.
Main_Event_Annotation: This is identified as a tornado event based on damage description.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind, even at F0 intensity, is the hazard.

Time_Annotation: July 13, 2004– A violent F4 tornado moved west of Roanoke, injuring 3 and completely destroying a parts supplier factory for Caterpillar Inc.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event is associated with the area west of Roanoke.
Main_Event_Annotation: The F4 intensity confirms a major tornado event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind is the destructive agent in this high-intensity tornado.

Event_Names: 2013 Tornado in Washington and Tazewell County
Time_Annotation: November 17, 2013– An unusually powerful EF4 tornado moved through Washington and several farmsteads in rural central Illinois, in Tazewell County, killing 3 and injuring 125.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The tornado affected areas in Washington and Tazewell County.
Main_Event_Annotation: An EF4 rating confirms this as a severe tornado event.
Hazards_Annotation: The hazard is the extreme wind speeds associated with an EF4 tornado.

Event_Names: 2015 Tornado in Ogle County (Rochelle and Fairdale)
Time_Annotation: April 9, 2015– A violent EF4 tornado moved through Ogle County, directly impacting the communities of Rochelle and Fairdale, killing 2 and injuring 22; it was the strongest tornado in northern Illinois in 25 years.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event highlights Ogle County, with specific mention of Rochelle and Fairdale.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EF4 classification confirms it as a major tornado.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage is the primary hazard in an EF4 tornado.

Time_Annotation: June 20, 2021– An EF3 tornado struck the Chicago suburbs of Naperville and Woodridge, damaging hundreds of structures, downing thousands of trees, and injuring 11 people; additionally, two EF0 tornadoes were reported near Romeoville and Addison.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The affected areas include Naperville, Woodridge, Romeoville, and Addison.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EF3 classification and additional EF0 events confirm this as a tornado outbreak.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage is the primary hazard associated with these tornadoes.

Time_Annotation: March 31 – April 31, 2023– An EF1 tornado struck the Apollo Theatre in Belvidere, causing the collapse of the structure onto a concert with 260 people, injuring 40 and killing 1; an accompanying EF3 tornado produced damage in Illinois before crossing into Indiana.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event primarily affected Belvidere and later impacted areas in Indiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EF1 and EF3 ratings confirm this tornado event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind, causing structural collapse and widespread damage, is the hazard.

Event_Names: 2023 Tornado near Marcelline, Jackson, and Jasper Counties
Time_Annotation: August 5, 2023– A relatively brief EF2 tornado tracked 2.87 miles near Marcelline, damaging numerous homes and downing power lines; additionally, an EF0 tornado affected Jackson County and another EF0 was observed in Jasper County.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The affected areas include near Marcelline, Jackson County, and Jasper County.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EF2 rating along with subsequent EF0 events indicate tornado activity.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind is the destructive hazard in these tornadoes.

Event_Names: 2023 Tornado in Hancock County and near Pawnee
Time_Annotation: August 6, 2023– A multi-vortex EFU tornado moved 8 miles through Hancock County, causing no damage, while a strong EF2 tornado damaged several homes north of Pawnee.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event mentions Hancock County and an area north of Pawnee.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EFU and EF2 designations indicate tornado events.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage is the associated hazard with these tornadoes.
